nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What role does scrutiny play in the approach outlined in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: Scrutiny is a grounding aspect of the approach, as it involves examining taken-for-granted social conditions and assumptions to explore alternatives to the current social order.
nodes.paragraph: It is an analysis based in the deep-seated interrogation that lies at the heart of scientific inquiry and the manner to address sustainability problems, irrespective of the ideological con - frontations or the powerful actors it challenges, whether they be in the political, economic, or scientific realms. A grounding aspect of this approach is its scrutinty of taken-for-granted social conditions and assumptions. A criti- cal analysis is one that judiciously examines the prevailing social order and takes seriously the possibility and even the necessity for alternatives (Marcuse 2013). As such, it is indispensable for what contemporary sustainability science often refers to as sustainability transitions or transformations (e.g., Alonso-Adame et al. 2024; Davelaar 2021; Sahle et al. 2024a, b). Critical sustainability science draws fundamentally on the logic of science, even though it can and often does interrogate the institution of science (York 2021; York and Clark 2010). Importantly, in opposition to other cul- turally based critical approaches including for example post-structuralist, -modernist, -humanist, -Marxist criti- cal sustainability science is erected on a realist/materialist and dialectical footing.

nodes.question: What will be the first chapter discussed after the introduction of governance?
nodes.answer: The first chapter discussed after the introduction of governance will be about the methodology of the study.
nodes.paragraph: This includes understanding the interactionsbetween various measures, policies, and actors within the city (Casta n Broto & Westman, 2020 ; Wang & Ran, 2023 ). In order to address this research gap, it is useful to draw on the concept of governance, which will be discussed in greater detail in the following chapter (2). After a short sketch of the methodology of the study (chapter 3), wepresent (in chapter 4) key developments in local adminis- tration and urban society. On this basis, we focus (in chapter 5) on an attempt to classify the central forms ofinteraction and cooperation that we found traditional ones revitalised and new ones emerging. In the nal sum up (in chapter 6), we will come back to a question raised butnot explicitly addressed by our overview and stocktaking: To what degree does a more interactive governance, as we have observed it, also mean a more democraticgovernance?Interactive Governance Cornerstones of an Analytical Concept Interactivity: The Common Basic Idea of Various Concepts for a new Governance When one speaks of governance instead of government, one emphasises the processes of governing, including thevarious ways actors from the social sphere participate.

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What does the text suggest is needed for a shift towards co-operative action in governance?
nodes.answer: The text suggests that a shift towards cooperative action requires reorientation and restructuring efforts from all stakeholders involved, including administrators, citizens, and politicians.
nodes.paragraph: While the accent in the debate on interactive gover- nance is on the intersectoral, it is equally important to strive for more interaction within the administrative sector itself. The concern with this task is often debatedin terms of challenging the strict separation of different public administrations as silos (Scott & Gong, 2021 ). This leads to coordination problems due to theindividual perspectives and priorities of each organisa- tional unit, which do not share this information (Bogumil & Jann, 2020 ; Hustedt & Radtke, 2024 ). This is particularly evident when a new eld of action such as climate politics emerges, challenging already existing goals and routines across policy areas anddepartments. A shift towards a more co-operative style of action requires reorientation and restructuring steps on allsides (Tuurnas et al., 2023 ) stakeholders and admin- istrators, citizens and politicians. Political organisations and bodies (local councils and elected of cials) as wellas administrations need to open up statehood further to stakeholders from civil society and business. Likewise, civil society organisations cannot just simply regard themselves as a counter-power limiting itself toorganising pressure from below or from outside .
